text:
Context: The foundation stone for India’s first port-based e-methanol facility was laid at Deendayal Port, Kandla, Gujarat.

The ₹2,300 crore project will produce 150 tonnes daily to fuel international cargo vessels along the Asia–Europe trade corridor.

About India’s First Port-Based e-Methanol Production Facility:

What it is?

A state-of-the-art port-integrated industrial plant designed to produce synthetic, carbon-neutral e-methanol (green methanol) by synthesising green hydrogen generated from renewable electricity with captured biogenic carbon dioxide (CO2).

Organisation: Developed as a joint venture between the Deendayal Port Authority (DPA) under the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways (MoPSW) and Namrup-based state PSU Assam Petro-Chemicals Ltd. (APCL), structured under a 76:24 capital contribution ratio.

Located in: Kandla, Gandhidham, Kutch district, Gujarat, sited across 75 acres of port land directly within the logistics zone of the Deendayal Port.

Aim: To decarbonise the maritime shipping sector, transform India into a leading exporter of low-carbon green bunker fuels along the critical Singapore–Rotterdam maritime lane, and accelerate progress toward India’s Net Zero emissions target by 2070.

Key Features:

150 TPD Phased Scalable Modular Capacity: Executed in two phases: Phase I injects ₹1,200 crore to establish 50 tonnes per day (TPD) capacity by January 2027, followed by Phase II adding 100 TPD at ₹1,100 crore by March 2027.

Green Feedstock & Circular Inputs: Relies on dedicated renewable power, on-site desalinated water for green hydrogen electrolysis, and captured biogenic CO2 emissions to produce drop-in marine fuel.

Cost Competitiveness: Engineered to produce green methanol at a benchmark production cost of US$750 per tonne, substantially undercutting current international market prices of approximately US$1,300 per tonne.

Direct DPA Equity & Infrastructure Support: The Deendayal Port Authority contributes an equity stake of ₹567.32 crore, 75 acres of land, dedicated desalinated water pipelines, and renewable energy infrastructure.

Large-Scale Employment Generation: Projected to generate over 3,500 direct and indirect jobs, while building an integrated green molecules ecosystem spanning storage, pipeline transport, bunkering infrastructure, and downstream services.

description:
By Suryakanta ଆମେରିକା ରାଷ୍ଟ୍ରପତି ଡୋନାଲ୍ଡ ଟ୍ରମ୍ପ ଜାତିସଂଘ ସାଧାରଣ ପରିଷଦ (UNGA) ରେ ନିଜର ଅଭିଭାଷଣ ସମୟରେ ଆନ୍ତର୍ଜାତୀୟ ସାମୁଦ୍ରିକ ସଂଗଠନ (IMO) ର ଏକ ଯୋଜନା ଉପରେ ବର୍ଷିଛନ୍ତି। ବିଶ୍ୱବ୍ୟାପୀ ସିପିଂ ବା ଜାହାଜ ଚଳାଚଳ କ୍ଷେତ୍ରରୁ ଗ୍ରୀନହାଉସ୍ ଗ୍ୟାସ୍ ନିର୍ଗମନ ହ୍ରାସ କରିବାକୁ ପ୍ରସ୍ତୁତ ହୋଇଥିବା ଏହି ଯୋଜନାକୁ ସେ "ପ୍ରଥମ ବିଶ୍ୱସ୍ତରୀୟ କାର୍ବନ ଟ୍ୟାକ୍ସ" ବୋଲି ଅଭିହିତ କରିଛନ୍ତି। ଏହା ସହିତ ତାଙ୍କ ପ୍ରଶାସନ ହସ୍ତକ୍ଷେପ କରି ଏହାକୁ ବନ୍ଦ କରିବାରେ ସଫଳ ହୋଇଥିଲା ବୋଲି ସେ ଦାବି କରିଛନ୍ତି। ଟ୍ରମ୍ପଙ୍କ 'କାର୍ବନ ଟ୍ୟାକ୍ସ' ଦାବି ଟ୍ରମ୍ପ କହିଛନ୍ତି ଯେ, ଗତବର୍ଷ ଏକ ଅପରିଚିତ ଜାତିସଂଘ ସଂସ୍ଥାକୁ ଗୋପନରେ ବିଶ୍ୱର ପ୍ରଥମ କାର୍ବନ ଟ୍ୟାକ୍ସ ଲାଗୁ କରିବାରୁ ରୋକିବା ପାଇଁ ତାଙ୍କ ପ୍ରଶାସନ ହସ୍ତକ୍ଷେପ କରିବାକୁ ବାଧ୍ୟ ହୋଇଥିଲା। ତାଙ୍କ ମତରେ ଏହି ଟିକସ ଲାଗୁ ହୋଇଥିଲେ ଆନ୍ତର୍ଜାତୀୟ ସିପିଂ ଖର୍ଚ୍ଚ ୧୦ ରୁ ୨୦ ପ୍ରତିଶତ କିମ୍ବା ତା'ଠାରୁ ଅଧିକ ବୃଦ୍ଧି ପାଇଥାନ୍ତା। ସେ ସ୍ପଷ୍ଟ କରିଛନ୍ତି ଯେ, "କୌଣସି ବିଶ୍ୱ ସରକାର ନାହିଁ, ଏବଂ ମୁଁ ରାଷ୍ଟ୍ରପତି ଥିବା ପର୍ଯ୍ୟନ୍ତ କୌଣସି ବିଶ୍ୱସ୍ତରୀୟ ଟିକସ ଲାଗୁ ହେବ ନାହିଁ।" ଆଇଏମଓ (IMO) ର ଯୋଜନା କ'ଣ ଥିଲା?
ପ୍ରକୃତରେ ଆଇଏମଓ ର 'ନେଟ୍-ଜିରୋ ଫ୍ରେମୱାର୍କ' କୁ ଆନୁଷ୍ଠାନିକ ଭାବରେ ଟିକସ ବୋଲି ବର୍ଗୀକୃତ କରାଯାଇନାହିଁ। ଏହାକୁ ଏକ 'ଗ୍ଲୋବାଲ୍ ପ୍ରାଇସିଂ ମେକାନିଜମ୍' କିମ୍ବା 'ଅର୍ଥନୈତିକ ପଦକ୍ଷେପ' ବୋଲି କୁହାଯାଇଛି। ଏହି ବ୍ୟବସ୍ଥା ଅଧୀନରେ ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକ ସେମାନଙ୍କ ନିର୍ଗମନ ପ୍ରଦର୍ଶନ ଆଧାରରେ ଦେୟ ପ୍ରଦାନ କରିବେ। ଏହି ଅର୍ଥ ଏକ ପ୍ରସ୍ତାବିତ IMO ନେଟ୍-ଜିରୋ ପାଣ୍ଠି କୁ ଯିବାର ବ୍ୟବସ୍ଥା ଥିଲା। ୨୦୨୫ ଏପ୍ରିଲ୍ ରେ ବିଭିନ୍ନ ଦେଶ ଏହି ଯୋଜନାକୁ ନୀତିଗତ ଭାବେ ସମ୍ମତି ଦେଇଥିଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ ଆମେରିକାର ବିରୋଧ କାରଣରୁ ଏହା ସ୍ଥଗିତ ହୋଇଯାଇଥିଲା ଏବଂ ଆସନ୍ତା ଡିସେମ୍ବର ମାସରେ ଏହା ଉପରେ ପୁଣିଥରେ ଆଲୋଚନା ଆରମ୍ଭ ହେବ। ନିୟମ ଓ ପରିବେଶ ଉପରେ ପ୍ରଭାବ ଏହି ଯୋଜନାରେ ନିର୍ଦ୍ଧାରିତ ମାତ୍ରାଠାରୁ ଅଧିକ ଗ୍ରୀନହାଉସ୍ ଗ୍ୟାସ୍ ନିର୍ଗମନ କରୁଥିବା ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକୁ କ୍ଷତିପୂରଣ ଦେବାକୁ ପଡ଼ିବ, ଯେତେବେଳେ କି ଶୂନ୍ୟ ନିର୍ଗମନ ଜ୍ଞାନକୌଶଳ ବ୍ୟବହାର କରୁଥିବା ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକୁ ଆର୍ଥିକ ପୁରସ୍କାର ମିଳିବ। ଏହି ନିୟମଗୁଡ଼ିକ ମୁଖ୍ୟତଃ ୫,୦୦୦ ଗ୍ରସ୍ ଟନ୍ ରୁ ଅଧିକ ଓଜନର ବୃହତ୍ ସାମୁଦ୍ରିକ ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକ ଉପରେ ଲାଗୁ ହେବାର ଥିଲା, ଯାହାକି ଆନ୍ତର୍ଜାତୀୟ ସିପିଂରେ ମୋଟ କାର୍ବନ ନିର୍ଗମନର ୮୫ ପ୍ରତିଶତ ପାଇଁ ଦାୟୀ। ସୂଚନାଯୋଗ୍ୟ ଯେ, ବିଶ୍ୱବ୍ୟାପୀ ମୋଟ ଗ୍ରୀନହାଉସ୍ ନିର୍ଗମନର ୨ ପ୍ରତିଶତ କେବଳ ଆନ୍ତର୍ଜାତୀୟ ସିପିଂ କ୍ଷେତ୍ରରୁ ଆସିଥାଏ। ତେଣୁ, ୨୦୫୦ ସୁଦ୍ଧା ସିପିଂ ଶିଳ୍ପକୁ 'ନେଟ୍-ଜିରୋ' ନିର୍ଗମନ ଲକ୍ଷ୍ୟରେ ପହଞ୍ଚାଇବା ପାଇଁ IMO ଏହି ମହତ୍ତ୍ୱାକାଂକ୍ଷୀ ପଦକ୍ଷେପ ଗ୍ରହଣ କରିଥିଲା। About The Author: Suryakanta

ଆଇଏମଓ (IMO) ର ଯୋଜନା କ'ଣ ଥିଲା?

ପ୍ରକୃତରେ ଆଇଏମଓ ର 'ନେଟ୍-ଜିରୋ ଫ୍ରେମୱାର୍କ' କୁ ଆନୁଷ୍ଠାନିକ ଭାବରେ ଟିକସ ବୋଲି ବର୍ଗୀକୃତ କରାଯାଇନାହିଁ। ଏହାକୁ ଏକ 'ଗ୍ଲୋବାଲ୍ ପ୍ରାଇସିଂ ମେକାନିଜମ୍' କିମ୍ବା 'ଅର୍ଥନୈତିକ ପଦକ୍ଷେପ' ବୋଲି କୁହାଯାଇଛି। ଏହି ବ୍ୟବସ୍ଥା ଅଧୀନରେ ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକ ସେମାନଙ୍କ ନିର୍ଗମନ ପ୍ରଦର୍ଶନ ଆଧାରରେ ଦେୟ ପ୍ରଦାନ କରିବେ। ଏହି ଅର୍ଥ ଏକ ପ୍ରସ୍ତାବିତ IMO ନେଟ୍-ଜିରୋ ପାଣ୍ଠି କୁ ଯିବାର ବ୍ୟବସ୍ଥା ଥିଲା। ୨୦୨୫ ଏପ୍ରିଲ୍ ରେ ବିଭିନ୍ନ ଦେଶ ଏହି ଯୋଜନାକୁ ନୀତିଗତ ଭାବେ ସମ୍ମତି ଦେଇଥିଲେ ମଧ୍ୟ ଆମେରିକାର ବିରୋଧ କାରଣରୁ ଏହା ସ୍ଥଗିତ ହୋଇଯାଇଥିଲା ଏବଂ ଆସନ୍ତା ଡିସେମ୍ବର ମାସରେ ଏହା ଉପରେ ପୁଣିଥରେ ଆଲୋଚନା ଆରମ୍ଭ ହେବ।

ନିୟମ ଓ ପରିବେଶ ଉପରେ ପ୍ରଭାବ

ଏହି ଯୋଜନାରେ ନିର୍ଦ୍ଧାରିତ ମାତ୍ରାଠାରୁ ଅଧିକ ଗ୍ରୀନହାଉସ୍ ଗ୍ୟାସ୍ ନିର୍ଗମନ କରୁଥିବା ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକୁ କ୍ଷତିପୂରଣ ଦେବାକୁ ପଡ଼ିବ, ଯେତେବେଳେ କି ଶୂନ୍ୟ ନିର୍ଗମନ ଜ୍ଞାନକୌଶଳ ବ୍ୟବହାର କରୁଥିବା ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକୁ ଆର୍ଥିକ ପୁରସ୍କାର ମିଳିବ। ଏହି ନିୟମଗୁଡ଼ିକ ମୁଖ୍ୟତଃ ୫,୦୦୦ ଗ୍ରସ୍ ଟନ୍ ରୁ ଅଧିକ ଓଜନର ବୃହତ୍ ସାମୁଦ୍ରିକ ଜାହାଜଗୁଡ଼ିକ ଉପରେ ଲାଗୁ ହେବାର ଥିଲା, ଯାହାକି ଆନ୍ତର୍ଜାତୀୟ ସିପିଂରେ ମୋଟ କାର୍ବନ ନିର୍ଗମନର ୮୫ ପ୍ରତିଶତ ପାଇଁ ଦାୟୀ। ସୂଚନାଯୋଗ୍ୟ ଯେ, ବିଶ୍ୱବ୍ୟାପୀ ମୋଟ ଗ୍ରୀନହାଉସ୍ ନିର୍ଗମନର ୨ ପ୍ରତିଶତ କେବଳ ଆନ୍ତର୍ଜାତୀୟ ସିପିଂ କ୍ଷେତ୍ରରୁ ଆସିଥାଏ। ତେଣୁ, ୨୦୫୦ ସୁଦ୍ଧା ସିପିଂ ଶିଳ୍ପକୁ 'ନେଟ୍-ଜିରୋ' ନିର୍ଗମନ ଲକ୍ଷ୍ୟରେ ପହଞ୍ଚାଇବା ପାଇଁ IMO ଏହି ମହତ୍ତ୍ୱାକାଂକ୍ଷୀ ପଦକ୍ଷେପ ଗ୍ରହଣ କରିଥିଲା।

The IMO’s Research and Development Forum has examined how the growing use of alternative marine fuels could change pollution-response requirements.

Held on September 21-22 in Singapore, the forum brought together regulators, scientists, industry representatives and emergency responders to discuss preparedness for incidents involving newer marine fuels.

Hosted by Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore, with support from China, the event covered LNG, LPG, methanol, ammonia, hydrogen, biofuels and e-fuels.

Discussions focused on how the different properties of these fuels could affect spill behaviour and response strategies.

Participants also looked at spill modelling, risk assessment, emergency response, post-spill actions and international cooperation.

The forum included expert presentations, case studies, panel discussions and working sessions, allowing participants to share research and operational experience.

A key theme was the need for closer cooperation between governments, industry, academia and the scientific community to address knowledge gaps and improve preparedness before major incidents occur.

Participants also stressed the importance of using research findings, operational experience and international cooperation to develop response protocols for alternative fuels.

text:
The shipping industry will likely miss its 2030 targets for vessels running on alternative fuels, according to a new study from the UCL Energy Institute, mainly due to the regulatory uncertainties surrounding the IMO Net-Zero Framework (NZF).

According to the fifth edition of 'Climate action in shipping: Progress towards shipping's 2030 breakthrough', the industry is highly unlikely to meet targets of having zero-emission fuels accounting for 5-10 percent of total fuel usage, the goal set in the 2023 IMO Greenhouse Gas Strategy. The ultimate goal is to ensure the shipping industry becomes net-zero by 2050, and the 2030 target was conceived as an enabler to accelerate early progress.

The 2030 targets meant that some 600-1,200 large ships with a capacity of at least 15,000 TEU (or equivalent) would be running on scalable zero-emissions fuels (SZEF). However, owing to headwinds like economic and political upheaval, the Strait of Hormuz crisis, energy security and supply chain concerns, and the regulatory uncertainty caused by the failure to adopt the NZF, the world is lagging behind on its alternative fuel goals. In 2025, the milestone of having roughly 100 15,000-TEU-equivalent ships running on SZEF was not met.

The UCL Energy Institute and the Getting to Zero Coalition report shows that while the world is falling behind on its goals, there have been notable achievements across the five key 'levers' being used to assess the industry's progress - namely technology and supply, demand, finance, policy, and civil society.

Supply of alternative fuels and technologies has, for instance, been progressing. The number of ports offering methanol bunkering now stands at 29, up from 19 a year ago. The world has also witnessed sea trials of the first large ammonia-fueled vessels with two-stroke engines being successfully completed, as well as the building of smaller ammonia-fueled supply vessels and tugboats fitted with four-stroke engines. The industry has also recorded its first ship-to-ship ammonia bunkering operation.

The report shows that the long-anticipated wave of methanol-capable container ship deliveries finally landed in 2025, tripling methanol-capable in-service tonnage from 2.3 million to 7.7 million gross tonnage (GT) and pushing the SZEF-capable share of the active fleet from 0.41 percent to 0.77 percent. This was the largest single-year capability gain on record, delivered through 56 newbuilds totaling 5.4 million GT. However, the order book regressed, with SZEF-capable orders falling from 9.5 percent to 5.7 percent of total GT orders.

On finance, the progress has been mixed: issuances of shipping-specific sustainable debt have plateaued. In 2025, approximately $3 billion was issued to shipping-related entities through green loans, green bonds, sustainability-linked loans, and transition instruments, down from $3.4 billion in 2024.

For the industry, the controversies surrounding the NZF have become one of the major roadblocks towards the 2030 goals, with the U.S. being among its staunchest opponents. The report reckons that with the NZF remaining in limbo, the policy clarity required for the 2030 goal is a major obstacle.

“The failure to adopt the NZF was the single most transition-regressive event we've seen in the five years this report has been running,” said Pinar Langer, research fellow at the UCL Energy Institute.

She added that reversing this momentum loss and securing regulatory certainty is one of the most important next steps to give shipowners the confidence to order zero-emission vessels, lenders the incentive to invest in them, and charterers the motivation to pay for low-carbon shipping.

text:
The number of B100 samples ENGINE recorded in Rotterdam more than doubled in the first eight months of 2026 from a year earlier, lifting its share of the port’s biofuel samples to almost a quarter.

ENGINE recorded 77 B100 fuel quality samples in Rotterdam between January and August, up 126% from 34 in the same period last year.

In total, ENGINE had data for 342 biofuel samples in Rotterdam between January and August 2026, up from 275 in the same period of 2025.

ENGINE’s sample data covers only part of Rotterdam’s biofuel bunker market. In the first half of 2026, suppliers in the Dutch port sold around 345,000 mt of what the Port of Rotterdam Authority classes as bio-blended fuel oils and distillates.

ENGINE’s samples for the same period cover around 135,000 mt, or 39%, of those sales. Some samples do not have a quantity recorded, so actual coverage is somewhat higher.

The port authority does not report B100 sales as a separate category, so no official B100 figures exist for the port. The number of B100 samples in ENGINE’s data can therefore act as an indicator of how demand for the fuel is trending in Rotterdam.

B100’s share of Rotterdam’s biofuel samples rose to 23% in the first eight months of 2026, from 12% in the same period of 2025.

Most other biofuel grades lost share. B30-VLSFO accounted for 28% of samples, down from 37%. B30-LSMGO’s share slipped from 22% to 20%, and B30-HSFO’s fell from 7% to 3%.

B30-ULSFO was the only other grade to gain share, rising from 22% to 27%.

Rotterdam is currently the largest bunker hub in the world by marine biofuel volumes. The port’s demand is supported by the Netherlands’ implementation of the EU’s RED III directive, which incentivises bunkering of biofuels, making them considerably cheaper in Rotterdam than in other European ports.

Under Dutch rules, bunker suppliers in the country’s ports can generate maritime emission reduction units, known as ZRE A tickets, by selling low-emission marine fuels such as biofuels made from advanced feedstocks listed in the directive, including palm oil mill effluent.

These ZRE A tickets can then be sold to suppliers of conventional fuels such as VLSFO or LSMGO, who need them to meet their own obligations.

The EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) and FuelEU Maritime add a further pull, as both reward shipowners for burning biofuel with lower carbon costs and smaller compliance penalties.

ENGINE’s samples show 15 bunker suppliers selling biofuels in Rotterdam in the first eight months of 2026, up from 10 in the same period last year. The number selling B100 rose from three to seven.

title: Assam boosts industrial footprint with e-methanol project at Kandla | Daily Pioneer
description:

Speaking on the occasion, Chief Minister Sarma said that the project would contribute significantly to India’s efforts to expand the use of green fuels.
The Chief Minister also highlighted the deep historical and contemporary ties between Assam and Gujarat.
He noted that Assam is India’s largest tea-producing State, while Gujarat is among the major markets for Assam tea.

text:
Strengthening Assam’s growing industrial presence at the national level, Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma along with Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel and Union Minister for Ports Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal formally laid the foundation stone for a major e-methanol production project at Kandla in Gujarat at Kandla in Gujarat today.

The project is a joint initiative of Assam Petro-Chemicals Limited (APCL) and the Deendayal Port Authority.

With an investment of Rs 2,300 crore and a production capacity of 150 tonnes per day (TPD), the project is among the major e-methanol production initiatives in the country. It is expected to create more than 3,500 direct and indirect employment opportunities. To be established at Kandla Port, one of India’s major maritime commercial hubs on the western coast, the project is envisaged to promote the use of green fuel in the shipping sector, reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels and contribute to lowering emissions from maritime transport. The project also marks a significant expansion of Assam’s industrial footprint beyond the State and reflects the capabilities and growing role of Assam’s public sector enterprises in emerging areas of the national green economy.

Speaking on the occasion, Chief Minister Sarma said that the project would contribute significantly to India’s efforts to expand the use of green fuels. He recalled Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s commitment to achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2070, announced at the United Nations Climate Change Conference in Glasgow in 2021.

The Chief Minister said that, in keeping with the Prime Minister’s vision, India has witnessed the emergence of a new movement towards green fuels and clean energy. He stated that Gujarat has emerged as a leading State in this transition through initiatives in solar power, green hydrogen and other forms of clean energy. Sarma said that the Prime Minister’s vision of accelerating the adoption of green fuels is gradually being translated into action across the country and that India is making significant strides in the development and adoption of clean energy technologies.

He said that it is heartening that the shipping sector is also being brought within the ambit of this green transition. In this context, the e-methanol project at Kandla assumes particular significance, as the methanol produced through the project is envisaged to be used as a marine fuel for ships operating from the port to international destinations.

Highlighting Assam’s historic contribution to India’s energy sector, Sarma said that the State has played a pioneering role in the country’s oil and petroleum industry. He pointed out that Asia’s first mechanically drilled oil well was established at Makum in Assam in 1867, while India’s first oil refinery was commissioned at Digboi in 1901.

He said that Assam continues to make an important contribution to the country’s oil and natural gas sector. and also possesses considerable experience in methanol production.

Assam Petro-Chemicals Limited at Namrup has a methanol production capacity of up to 500 tonnes per day, providing the State with valuable expertise in the sector. Stating the invitation extended by Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal to Assam Petro-Chemicals Limited to participate as a partner in the Kandla e-methanol project, Dr. Sarma said that Assam readily accepted the opportunity, considering it a matter of pride for the State to contribute to one of the country’s major green-fuel initiatives.

He expressed hope that similar green-fuel projects would be developed at other major ports across the country in the coming years, further strengthening India’s transition towards cleaner and more sustainable maritime transportation. The Chief Minister also highlighted the deep historical and contemporary ties between Assam and Gujarat. Referring to the ancient connection associated with Lord Krishna and Rukmini, he said that the relationship between the two States has continued to grow in modern times as well. He noted that Assam is India’s largest tea-producing State, while Gujarat is among the major markets for Assam tea.

Dr. Sarma further informed that senior officials from Assam had recently visited the Gujarat State Secretariat to gain a deeper understanding of Gujarat’s development experience and institutional practices, with the objective of drawing lessons relevant to Assam’s own development journey. Reflecting on the transformation of Assam and the Northeast, the Chief Minister said that the region, once perceived as one of the deprived parts of the country, is witnessing a significant change in its development trajectory in recent years.

He pointed to the emergence of new industrial and technological initiatives, including semiconductor-related projects, as evidence of the changing economic landscape of Assam and the Northeast. Dr. Sarma said, “I would like to thank the people of Gujarat for giving India a Prime Minister whom the people of the Northeast had always been waiting for. Under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the transformation of Assam and the Northeast is progressing at full speed today.”

The Chief Minister expressed his gratitude to Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel and Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal for facilitating Assam’s participation in the landmark e-methanol project and for strengthening the industrial partnership between Assam and Gujarat.

Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal and Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel were present at the programme.

Gujarat Minister of State for Labour, Skill Development and Employment Kantilal Amrutiya, Minister of State for Higher and Technical Education Trikam Chhanga, Kachchh Lok Sabha MP Vinod Chavda, Gandhidham MLA Malti Ben Kishor Maheshwari, Naharkatia MLA and Political Secretary to the Chief Minister Taranga Gogoi, Chairman, Deendayal Port Authority, Sushil Kumar Singh, Chairman, Assam Petro-Chemicals Limited, Bikul Deka, and host of other dignitaries were present on the occasion.

text:
US President Donald Trump used his address to the United Nations General Assembly earlier in the week to attack a plan by the International Maritime Organization (IMO) to cut greenhouse gas emissions from global shipping. He called it a “first-ever global carbon tax” that his administration had stepped in to stop.

“Last year, my administration was forced to intervene to stop an obscure UN body, the International Maritime Organization, from secretly establishing a first-ever global carbon tax – very expensive tax – to raise international shipping costs by 10 to 20%, and maybe even more than that,” Trump said. “There is no global government, and while I'm president, there will be no global taxes,” he claimed.

The IMO’s Net-Zero Framework (NZF) is not formally classified as a tax. It pairs mandatory emissions standards for ships with a global greenhouse gas pricing mechanism. Countries agreed to it in principle in April 2025, but opposition led by the US has delayed its formal adoption, and it remains under negotiation.

Also read: Himalayan glaciers melting 65% faster, black carbon to blame: Study

IMO and the shipping industry

The IMO is the UN’s specialised agency for regulating international shipping. The organisation has worked on carbon emissions from ships for decades, and its member states first voted on a resolution to address carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions in 1997.

In 2011, the IMO introduced the Energy Efficiency Design Index, which set mandatory efficiency standards for new ships. Member states adopted an initial greenhouse gas strategy in 2018. They followed it in 2023 with a more ambitious strategy, which calls for international shipping to reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions “by or around 2050”, with interim targets for 2030 and 2040.

International shipping accounts for more than 2% of global emissions, according to the climate policy website Carbon Brief. It is not directly covered by the emissions targets of the Paris Agreement.

The Net-Zero Framework

The IMO drew up the framework to turn its 2023 climate ambitions into binding rules for the industry. The version its Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) approved in April 2025 has two parts: a global fuel standard and an economic measure tied to greenhouse gas emissions.

The fuel standard would require ships to progressively cut their greenhouse gas fuel intensity, the amount of greenhouse gases they emit for each unit of energy they use.

Under the economic measure, ships that exceed specified emissions-intensity thresholds would have to acquire “remedial units” to cover the shortfall. Ships running on zero- or near-zero-emission technologies could instead become eligible for financial rewards. Ships with surplus compliance units could transfer them to other vessels or bank them for later use.

The rules would apply to large ocean-going ships above 5,000 gross tonnage, which the IMO says account for about 85% of CO2 emissions from international shipping.

Also read: Why carbon markets cannot close India’s nature-finance gap

Trump calls it a ‘carbon tax’

The IMO calls the proposal a “global pricing mechanism” and an “economic measure”, under which ships make payments linked to their emissions performance. Those payments could still add up to a substantial revenue stream, which Carbon Brief reported would flow into a proposed IMO Net-Zero Fund.

The framework sets two intensity targets each year, a stricter “direct compliance” target and a looser “base” target. A ship that meets the base target but misses the stricter one covers the gap with Tier 1 units. A ship that misses the base target must also buy the costlier Tier 2 units for its emissions above that line.

Carbon Brief reported prices of $100 per Tier 1 unit and $380 per Tier 2 unit. Each unit covers one tonne of CO2-equivalent.

The fund was estimated to raise about $10 billion to $15 billion a year in its early years. The money would support low-emission ships and the development of cleaner fuels, and pay for research, infrastructure, training and technology transfer.

The IMO said the fund would also help mitigate the effects of the transition on vulnerable countries, including small island developing states and least developed countries.

Also read: India knows where the rain falls, but still can't tell a village to run

The US hurdle

The US withdrew from the negotiations midway through the April 2025 meeting, but countries still agreed to the framework in principle. According to Carbon Brief, 63 countries voted in favour, including the European Union, China, India and Brazil. Saudi Arabia, Russia and the UAE were among those that voted against.

Formal adoption was expected in October 2025. The Trump administration strongly opposed the framework and lobbied against its adoption. The same month, US secretary of state Marco Rubio and Sean Duffy, then the transportation secretary, warned governments that backing the framework could bring sanctions, tariffs, additional port fees or visa restrictions for crews.

“This will be the first time that a UN organisation levies a global carbon tax on the world,” Rubio and Duffy wrote in a joint letter, adding: “We will fight hard to protect our economic interests by imposing costs on countries if they support the NZF.”

The extraordinary IMO meeting that followed ended without the agreement needed to formally adopt the framework. Countries voted to adjourn, pushing the decision into 2026.

text:
BUSAN — The city of Busan is extending the stage for its next-generation nuclear industry from land to sea. The plan is to develop maritime small modular reactors (SMRs) as a future growth industry while pursuing designation as an SMR special zone, building a hub for next-generation nuclear power that spans both onshore and offshore applications.

Busan is conducting a study on the feasibility of and strategy for an SMR special zone designation, in line with the SMR Special Act that was enacted in March and took effect on the 11th of this month, the city said on the 27th. Based on the findings, the city plans to launch a research project next year to draw up and secure a Busan-style SMR special zone plan. It will also compete for a research and development special zone designation in line with the Ministry of Science and ICT's master plan for SMR system development.

To set itself apart from other regions, Busan is considering positioning the zone as a base for demonstration and exports. Rather than concentrating on research or manufacturing, the city aims to link its existing nuclear industry base with port and shipbuilding infrastructure to create an industrial ecosystem running from demonstration through to exports.

Maritime SMRs are the centerpiece of the plan. The technology applies small reactors to floating nuclear plants and nuclear-powered vessels. It is drawing attention as a way to meet rising data center power demand driven by the spread of artificial intelligence, tighter carbon emissions rules from the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the opening of Arctic shipping routes.

Busan hosts a cluster of port infrastructure including the Busan New Port, along with shipbuilding and marine industries and a supply chain for nuclear power equipment. To connect these assets to the maritime SMR industry, the city has held seminars on fostering maritime SMRs and meetings of a nuclear industry working group to gather views from experts and industry. It plans to form a maritime SMR forum and council to broaden cooperation among government, industry, academia and research institutes, together with the private sector.

Commercializing maritime SMRs is a medium- to long-term undertaking that will require technology development, safety verification and the establishment of international regulatory standards. "Maritime SMRs should not be approached as a business to be commercialized in a short period," a Busan city official said. "It is a medium- to long-term industry that requires technology development, safety verification, the establishment of international regulatory standards, and the securing of supply chains and manpower all at the same time."

The city's existing nuclear industry base is also expanding into SMRs. Gijang County in Busan was selected as the site for the country's first i-SMR demonstration project. With the operation of the Kori nuclear power plant, the decommissioning of Kori Unit 1, a support center for manufacturing SMR auxiliary equipment and now a next-generation reactor demonstration, Busan has assembled a nuclear industry base covering operations, decommissioning, manufacturing and demonstration.

Going forward, the city plans to pursue the special zone designation while expanding the related industrial base through the maritime SMR forum and council. "Maritime SMRs are a medium- to long-term national strategic industry for responding to carbon neutrality, the shift to eco-friendly vessels and the AI era," a city official said. "We will pull together the region's industrial and research capabilities to win the special zone designation and gain an early foothold in the global supply chain."

Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma, Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel and Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal on Friday laid the foundation stone for a Rs 2,300-crore e-methanol project at Kandla in Gujarat, marking a major industrial partnership between Assam and Gujarat.

The project is a joint initiative of Assam Petro-Chemicals Limited (APCL) and the Deendayal Port Authority. It will have a production capacity of 150 tonnes of e-methanol per day and is expected to generate more than 3,500 direct and indirect employment opportunities.

The facility will come up at Kandla Port, one of India's major commercial ports on the western coast. The e-methanol produced at the facility is expected to be used as marine fuel for ships operating from the port to international destinations.

The project is aimed at promoting cleaner fuel in the shipping sector and reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels. It is also expected to support efforts to reduce emissions from maritime transport.

Speaking at the foundation stone-laying ceremony, Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma said Assam's participation in the project was a matter of pride for the state. He said the initiative would contribute to India's efforts to expand the use of green fuels.

CM Sarma referred to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's commitment to achieving net-zero carbon emissions by 2070 and said the country was moving towards greater use of clean energy.

He also highlighted Gujarat's role in the development of solar power, green hydrogen and other clean-energy initiatives.

Assam's Oil Legacy And Methanol Experience

CM Sarma pointed to Assam's long association with India's oil and petroleum industry while explaining the state's role in the new project.

He said Asia's first mechanically drilled oil well was established at Makum in Assam in 1867, while India's first oil refinery was commissioned at Digboi in 1901.

Assam also has experience in methanol production through Assam Petro-Chemicals Limited at Namrup, which has a production capacity of up to 500 tonnes per day, according to the state government.

Assam CM said APCL agreed to participate in the Kandla project after Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal invited the Assam-based company to become a partner in the initiative.

The Chief Minister expressed hope that similar green-fuel projects would come up at other major ports in the country, contributing to cleaner maritime transportation.

Assam-Gujarat Industrial Partnership

CM Sarma also spoke about the historical and economic ties between Assam and Gujarat. He noted that Assam is India's largest tea-producing state and Gujarat is among the major markets for Assam tea.

He said senior Assam government officials had recently visited the Gujarat State Secretariat to study the state's development experience and institutional practices, with the aim of applying relevant lessons to Assam.

The Chief Minister also referred to recent industrial and technology-related developments in Assam and the Northeast, including semiconductor-related projects, as signs of a changing economic landscape in the region.

Union Minister Sarbananda Sonowal and Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel attended the foundation stone-laying ceremony.

Gujarat Ministers of State Kantilal Amrutiya and Trikam Chhanga, Kachchh Lok Sabha MP Vinod Chavda, Gandhidham MLA Malti Ben Kishor Maheshwari, Naharkatia MLA and Political Secretary to the Chief Minister Taranga Gogoi, Deendayal Port Authority Chairman Sushil Kumar Singh and APCL Chairman Bikul Deka were also present.

text:
The International Maritime Organization is calling on Fiji and Pacific island countries to ensure maritime policies translate into practical improvements for the people who depend on shipping.

Speaking at Fiji’s World Maritime Day celebration, IMO Pacific Coordinator Sitalingi Payne says the success of maritime policies should be measured by the results they deliver on the ground.

He says for Fiji, maritime excellence must respond to the needs of its people, particularly communities that rely on inter-island shipping to access essential goods, schools, hospitals and markets.

“We must ask what has changed because of our policies. Are vessels safer? Are crews better prepared? Are port clearance simpler? And is the ocean better protected?”

Payne says vessels must be suited to local conditions, properly maintained and safely operated, while seafarers must be properly trained, fairly treated and supported in their work.

He is also calling for greater investment in maritime education and training as the industry prepares for new fuels, digital systems and cleaner shipping technologies.

IMO has called on stakeholders to carry three commitments forward — putting policies into action, strengthening partnerships and investing in people.

These efforts should ultimately result in safer voyages, cleaner seas and more reliable maritime services for Fiji and the wider Pacific.

text:
India has begun development of its first port-based e-methanol production facility at Deendayal Port Authority in Kandla, Gujarat, as part of wider efforts to decarbonise maritime transport and expand clean energy exports. The project, announced by the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, is intended to supply green fuel to ships operating on the Asia-Europe trade corridor. According to the official government announcement, the facility will also support India’s target of achieving net zero emissions by 2070.

Phased development planned at Kandla

The facility will have a total production capacity of 150 tonnes per day and will use renewable energy, water and carbon dioxide sourced from biological processes to produce e-methanol. The fuel is expected to support cleaner maritime transport and bunkering operations for vessels travelling along one of the world’s busiest shipping routes.

The project is a joint initiative between Deendayal Port Authority and Assam Petro-Chemicals Limited. It will be developed in phases, beginning with a 50-tonne-per-day unit scheduled for completion by January 2027. The second phase will add a further 100 tonnes per day, with completion targeted for March 2027.

Total investment in the project is valued at ₹2,300 crore (approximately US$276 million). Of this, ₹1,200 crore (approximately US$144 million) will be allocated to the first phase and ₹1,100 crore (approximately US$132 million) to the second phase. The capital contribution ratio between the two partners is 76:24.

Supporting maritime decarbonisation goals

The development forms part of India’s broader maritime modernisation strategy, which includes expanding domestic shipbuilding capacity and increasing the use of alternative fuels. The government has also outlined plans to add 100 new vessels to the country’s commercial fleet over the next five years and aims to position India among the world’s top five ship-owning nations by 2047.

Additional maritime infrastructure projects are also under way in Gujarat. These include a shipbuilding initiative at Vadinar and a proposed greenfield shipbuilding and repair cluster at Kuchhadi in Porbandar. The plans align with wider efforts described in India’s maritime capacity expansion programme.

Officials said the Kandla facility is expected to strengthen India’s role in the global green fuel supply chain. The government stated that production costs are estimated at around US$750 per tonne, compared with current international rates of about US$1,300 per tonne.

Employment and industrial impact

The project is expected to create more than 3,500 direct and indirect jobs across transport, storage, fuel production and related services. Deendayal Port Authority will contribute equity capital, land, desalinated water and renewable energy inputs, including green hydrogen.

The initiative also reflects India’s broader push towards energy self-reliance and industrial expansion in low-carbon sectors. Recent measures to strengthen energy and infrastructure systems include programmes such as India’s domestic PNG expansion scheme and investments in digital infrastructure supporting industrial growth.

Leaders highlight regional collaboration

“Under the leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, India is moving faster and greener than ever before, and Gujarat is proud to lead this journey. The long coastline of Kutch and Gujarat will now energise the world’s ships through Kandla. This plant converts our renewable energy capacity into exports and makes Gujarat’s coast India’s gateway of green energy for the world.” Bhupendra Patel, Chief Minister of Gujarat

“India is now building its own ships and containers, and soon it will also produce the clean fuel that powers global trade. In the coming years, Kandla will become a green fuel hub on the Singapore-Rotterdam route and this plant will serve as a model for every major port in the country.” Sarbananda Sonowal, Minister of Ports, Shipping and Waterways

Officials from Gujarat and Assam described the project as an example of inter-state cooperation linking industrial capacity, renewable resources and maritime infrastructure. The foundation ceremony was held at the Deendayal Port Authority exhibition grounds in Gandhidham.

text:
Kandla is set to strengthen its role in India’s green shipping drive with the foundation stone laid for a Rs 2,300-crore e-methanol plant at Deendayal Port. The 150-tonne-per-day facility is expected to create more than 3,500 direct and indirect jobs and support the development of cleaner marine fuels, reported the Blunt Times.

The project is being developed as a joint venture between the Deendayal Port Authority (DPA) and Assam Petro-chemicals Ltd (APL). Gujarat Chief Minister Bhupendra Patel and Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma laid the foundation stone at the DPA Exhibition Ground in Gandhidham. Union Minister for Ports, Shipping and Waterways Sarbananda Sonowal was also present.

Patel said the project would support India’s transition towards green energy by combining Gujarat’s maritime infrastructure with Assam’s industrial capabilities. He said the e-methanol facility would add momentum to the country’s green-energy ambitions.

Deendayal Port is being developed as a Green Hydrogen Hub under the National Green Hydrogen Mission, with infrastructure planned for the production, storage, handling and transportation of green hydrogen and its derivatives.

The e-methanol project could also support the decarbonisation of the maritime sector by providing an alternative fuel for ships and reducing reliance on conventional fossil fuels.

Sarma described the facility as a major industrial partnership between Gujarat and Assam and said the project could be expanded to support the use of green methanol in both domestic and international shipping.

With a production capacity of 150 tonnes per day, the plant is expected to generate employment across engineering, logistics, transportation, supply chains and related sectors.

Sonowal said the project would deepen economic ties between Gujarat and Assam while creating employment opportunities. He said the facility, developed in collaboration with central government institutions, would contribute to the two states’ industrial partnership.

Assam Petro-chemicals chairman Bikul Deka said domestic production of green marine fuel would support India’s energy security and the broader Atmanirbhar Bharat objective.

text:
Ammobia and Lummus Technology to Commercialize Ammonia for Low-Carbon Energy

Ammobia’s low-capex synthesis will power the first ammonia solution in Lummus’ portfolio, meeting ammonia demand for low-carbon maritime fuel and energy storage and transport

SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Ammobia, a developer of breakthrough low-cost, modular ammonia production technology, today announced an agreement with Lummus Technology, a global provider of process technologies and value-driven energy solutions, to license and deploy Ammobia’s ammonia production system. Through this partnership, Ammobia’s technology is to be deployed in commercial installations worldwide and used in integrated solutions that complement Lummus’ hydrogen portfolio, including marine fuels and energy storage and transport. Ammobia’s “Haber-Bosch 2.0” process will be the first ammonia technology in Lummus’ portfolio.

Ammobia and Lummus Technology held a signing ceremony at Ammobia’s HQ in San Francisco, CA, USA. From Left: Ilya L. Aranovich, EMBA, Vice President, Corporate Strategy, Lummus; Ronald Venner, Chief Business Officer, Growth & Strategic Accounts, Lummus; Karen Baert, Co-founder & CEO, Ammobia; Tristan Gilbert, Co-founder & CTO, Ammobia; Guido Radaelli, Chief Engineering Officer, Ammobia. Photo Credit: Ana Sofia Alcega

Rethinking Ammonia Production Economics: A Capital-Efficient Synthesis Loop Meets Global Scale

Lummus brings decades of experience in developing new technologies from initial concept to commercial scale with expertise in reactor, process and thermal design. By combining Ammobia’s capital-efficient synthesis loop (“synloop”) with Lummus engineering and technology expertise and global reach provides a low-risk, financeable pathway to production for a variety of in-demand use cases such as power generation.

Karen Baert, Co-founder and CEO of Ammobia, said:

Ammobia changes the economics of producing ammonia from any energy source and does it in modules rather than the world-scale plants that have defined this industry for a century

“Customers can add capacity through a greenfield project or an upgrade to an existing operating site. Lummus brings the engineering rigor, project delivery, and global relationships required to deploy it, which lets Ammobia stay focused on advancing the core process. Together we can make ammonia’s newest applications, from resilient power to clean maritime fuel, commercially viable.”

Ammonia Projects That Are Financeable, Flexible, and Faster to Deploy

Developers and operators can deploy Ammobia through Lummus with the option to leverage an integrated solution that embeds Ammobia within Lummus’ hydrogen portfolio. Benefits include:

Bankable projects with limited risk: Lummus’ extensive, proven performance and production guarantees stabilize plant development risks using Ammobia’s standardized, modular designs.

No billion-dollar price tag: Ammobia’s reengineered synloop significantly reduces the initial capex investment required and lowers overall ammonia production costs.

Freedom from a single feedstock: Ammobia’s synloop runs on any energy source and Lummus’ hydrogen technologies span feedstocks, so customers can build around the cheapest or most abundant local energy, including a range of gas reforming and electrolyzer technologies, both established and emerging, as well as geologic hydrogen and renewable energy sources.

Faster to deploy: Ammobia’s repeatable design, combined with Lummus’ engineering and project execution capabilities, enables the rapid delivery of new packaged units to global customers while reducing timelines and risks associated with conventional ammonia projects.

More ways to add capacity: Medium-scale, modular plants and retrofits using Ammobia’s designs, guaranteed and delivered by Lummus, create new ways to add capacity beyond the megaprojects that have long defined the ammonia industry.

Leon de Bruyn, President and Chief Executive Officer of Lummus Technology, said:

We have a long track record of partnering with innovators to scale breakthrough technologies that address the evolving needs of the global energy market,

“Ammobia’s technology is an important addition to Lummus’ portfolio and a leap forward for the industry. This cutting-edge solution has the power to transform ammonia production to be more economical and lower carbon, support emissions reductions in the shipping industry, and significantly reduce project costs.”

From Fertilizer to Fuel: A Market Projected to Grow 58% by 2033

Ammonia demand is growing well beyond its traditional chemical uses. It already forms the foundation of 70% of fertilizers, which are responsible for feeding half the world’s population. Grand View Research projects ammonia production increasing 58% by 2033, driven by emerging demand as a maritime fuel and for power generation.

Ammobia’s technology is engineered to serve this full range of end markets. The Lummus partnership focuses on the energy generation opportunity, where the two companies will work together to bring projects to market at scale. Ammobia continues to advance its technology across ammonia’s other major segments, including fertilizer and industrial production.

Energy Storage and Transport: Ammonia is one of the most practical ways to import and store low-carbon energy using existing infrastructure, giving Europe, Japan, and South Korea access to resilient energy. Ammobia’s low-cost synthesis makes ammonia’s use as a carbon-free fuel for power generation, an emerging source of demand, significantly more economical.

Maritime Fuel: Ammonia has emerged as a promising low-carbon shipping fuel, and the fleet is already forming. As of June 2026, 441 vessels on order or in the water are either ammonia-ready or ammonia-fueled. As that fleet grows the main challenge becomes securing cost-competitive supply. Ammobia’s production technology can help meet ammonia bunkering demand at prices competitive with conventional marine fuel.

Fertilizers: Agriculture remains ammonia’s largest market by volume, and one where modular production can help plants be located closer to where the product is used, reducing exposure to long, concentrated supply chains. Ammobia’s plants are designed for regional siting, reducing supply chain risk.

The companies will begin identifying their first commercial projects in the coming months, prioritizing power generation and maritime fuel.

title: The Week in Alt Fuels: The cold feet conundrum | Hellenic Shipping News Worldwide
description:
The energy sector is developing zero-emission bunker fuel supply and infrastructure to meet the IMO’s 2030 target of 5-10% uptake.
The assessment focuses on e-methanol and e-ammonia as scalable zero-emission fuels (SZEF) with a well-to-wake GHG intensity below 19 gCO2e/MJ.
It excludes e-methane because of its methane slip, as well as blue fuels produced from fossil feedstocks with carbon capture and storage.
The Zero Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance (ZEMBA) pools demand from cargo owners including Amazon, DSV, Google and Microsoft.
In other alt fuels news this week, US President Donald Trump has signalled that his administration intends to prevent the IMO from adopting a global emissions-pricing mechanism.
text:
The energy sector is developing zero-emission bunker fuel supply and infrastructure to meet the IMO’s 2030 target of 5-10% uptake. But vessel orders and commercial demand are struggling to keep pace.

The IMO wants zero- or near-zero-emission energy to account for at least 5% of international shipping’s energy consumption by 2030, striving for 10%.

But the shipping industry still has a long way to go to meet this ambition, probably even further than two years ago.

In September 2024, researchers at the UCL Energy Institute and the Getting to Zero Coalition, run by the Global Maritime Forum (GMF), found that fuel supply was partially on track but demand was lagging. Two years later, their September 2026 report suggests little has changed.

“In several cases, progress has not only slowed relative to previous years but regressed,” the 2026 report said.

The assessment focuses on e-methanol and e-ammonia as scalable zero-emission fuels (SZEF) with a well-to-wake GHG intensity below 19 gCO2e/MJ. It excludes e-methane because of its methane slip, as well as blue fuels produced from fossil feedstocks with carbon capture and storage.

The report said production of SZEF still has the potential to catch up by 2030, but weakening demand from shipowners and cargo owners risks leaving that potential untapped.

More ships, but where’s the demand?

DNV data shows that five ammonia-capable vessels are now in operation, up from two in September 2024, with another 41 on order for delivery by 2030, compared with 28 two years ago.

The operational methanol- and ethanol-capable fleet has roughly tripled from 53 to 160 vessels over the same period, but its orderbook has barely moved from 294 to 299.

“The 2024 shift away from conventional fuels thus appears to have been a one-off pulse driven by a few large operators rather than a structural break in ordering behaviour,” the GMF and UCL report noted.

But more fuel-capable vessels do not necessarily translate into higher green fuel consumption. The GMF and UCL report’s authors found that actual SZEF consumption on dual-fuel ships remains “negligible”.

Based on the current fleet and orderbook, vessels would have the capacity to consume only around 12 million mt/year of e-methanol and e-ammonia by 2030, measured in heavy fuel oil-equivalent. This falls short of the 15 million mt/year minimum needed to meet the IMO’s 5% target.

Cargo owners tighten purse strings

The other side of the demand equation doesn’t look much better.

A Boston Consulting Group (BCG) survey of 125 cargo owners, published in April, found that the average green premium they were willing to pay fell to 3% in 2025 from 4.5% in 2024. The share of respondents prepared to pay more than 20% extra for low-emission fuels dropped to zero from 3% over the same period.

Only 45% expected to be willing to pay a premium within the next five years, down from 65% in 2024.

High fuel costs relative to their commercial benefits were the most frequently cited barrier, combined with wider regulatory and economic uncertainty.

But waning willingness to pay does not mean all cargo owners have stopped paying for emissions reductions. Some are paying a premium for emissions reductions through book-and-claim arrangements, even if their own cargo travels on a conventionally fuelled vessel. These arrangements could help create demand for e-fuels.

For instance, DP World will use Hapag-Lloyd’s biofuel-based service to claim around 4,700 mtCO2e of emissions reductions. Gap will use Maersk’s biofuel- or bio-methanol-based service to purchase reductions for its European trade lanes.

Pooling demand offers another route.

The Zero Emission Maritime Buyers Alliance (ZEMBA) pools demand from cargo owners including Amazon, DSV, Google and Microsoft. Its second tender will support Hapag-Lloyd’s planned e-methanol deployment and North Sea Container Line’s e-ammonia-powered service.

Together, the shipping companies are expected to cut GHG emissions by around 120,000 mtCO2e over three years from 2027, with ZEMBA members purchasing the reductions through book-and-claim.

How ready is ready?

Shipowners are also keeping their fuel options open. Fuel-ready tonnage accounts for 2.48% of the active fleet, against just 0.77% already SZEF-capable, the GMF and UCL report’s authors found.

Höegh Autoliners recently ordered six LNG dual-fuel car carriers with notations for future conversion to ammonia and methanol, without specifying their level of readiness.

But fuel-ready does not mean fuel-capable. Höegh’s vessels will run on LNG or conventional fuels until converted. Other fuel-ready ships may continue using conventional fuels. Shipowners could also choose not to convert them at all.

And until the conversion takes place, these vessels cannot use the intended zero-emission fuels.

“The failure to adopt the NZF [Net-Zero Framework] was the single most transition-regressive event we’ve seen in the five years this report has been running,” said Pinar Langer, research fellow at the UCL Energy Institute.

Regulatory certainty this year is what it will take to win back vessel orders and investment, Langer argued. The IMO’s next chance to adopt the Net-Zero Framework comes in December.

In other alt fuels news this week, US President Donald Trump has signalled that his administration intends to prevent the IMO from adopting a global emissions-pricing mechanism. “There is no global government – and while I am President, there will be no global taxes,” he said.

Class society American Bureau of Shipping has granted approval in principle to the design of a 22,000-cbm ammonia bunker vessel.

title: New research shows how regulation could reshape shipping
description:

text:
Amid regulatory uncertainty, there is one key challenge to ensuring shipping meets its decarbonization goals: making the right decisions today. DNV’s latest edition of Maritime Forecast to 2050 explores how different scenarios could reshape fuel demand, investment decisions, and decarbonization pathways, helping shipowners to navigate uncertainty and build resilient fleets.

Shipping’s energy transition has entered a new phase. The technology options are increasingly well understood. LNG, methanol, biofuels, wind-assisted propulsion, and emerging ammonia solutions are no longer concepts but commercial realities. Yet despite this progress, shipowners face a more difficult challenge than ever: making investment decisions amid unprecedented regulatory uncertainty.

The 2026 edition of DNV’s Maritime Forecast to 2050 argues that uncertainty itself is now becoming one of the most important drivers of fleet strategy. “Decisions taken today on vessel design, retrofits, and fuel capability will determine competitiveness for decades, while the outcome of ongoing regulatory negotiations could significantly reshape the economics of shipping’s energy transition,” says Øyvind Sekkesæter, Senior Consultant at DNV and lead author of this year’s report. “Maritime Forecast to 2050 aims to assist that decision-making with our latest core insights and case study examples.”

Four regulatory scenarios could shape shipping very differently

This year’s Maritime Forecast takes a scenario-based approach, presenting four possible regulatory futures for shipping. These range from the full adoption of IMO’s initially approved Net-Zero Framework (NZF) to its rejection and prolonged political gridlock, while also exploring several intermediate outcomes, including a delayed or revised NZF and scenarios where regional regulations play a more prominent role in driving decarbonization. Rather than predicting which outcome is most likely, the scenarios illustrate how different regulatory futures could affect fuel demand, energy-efficiency uptake, investment signals, and fleet competitiveness.

Stronger global regulation accelerates demand for low-GHG fuels and increases the attractiveness of energy-efficiency measures, while the absence of such regulation slows market development. The result is a transition whose pace may vary significantly depending on future policy decisions.

“For shipowners, this means the challenge is no longer identifying a single fuel pathway that fits the operational profile of their fleet. Instead, it is preparing fleets that remain competitive across multiple possible futures,” Sekkesæter concludes.

Tapping the fleet’s efficiency potential

Fully realizing the fleet’s energy-saving potential requires improvements not only to newbuilds but also to existing ships through retrofits.

Installing energy-saving devices during scheduled dry-docking can be a highly cost-effective decarbonization strategy, as illustrated by the Maritime Forecast’s case study of a hypothetical 15-year-old 5,000 TEU containership (built in 2013).

This envisages USD 2.35 million being invested to retrofit the ship with hydrodynamic enhancements including a bow retrofit, propeller upgrade, and a propeller boss cap fin.

The vessel can achieve estimated fuel savings of around 16% under the modelling assumptions. Evaluating the investment under three price scenarios for low sulphur heavy fuel oil (LSHFO) results in payback periods from 1.4 years to 4.2 years.

A USD 10 million opportunity: The business case for ship retrofits is strengthening

In the above scenarios, the net present value of the net savings is projected to reach between USD 2 and 10 million by 2038. The investment case is further strengthened by rising compliance costs under regulatory schemes such as the European Union Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) and FuelEU Maritime, which were excluded from the baseline assumptions.

“The key takeaway from this study is that even a 15-year-old vessel can offer a compelling business case for retrofitting energy-saving measures. The report also reveals that, unlike fuel choices, efficiency improvements create value under every regulatory scenario,” highlights Sekkesæter. At fleet level, the implications are substantial.

Operational excellence and quantifying real-world performance

Of course, shipowners making multi-million-dollar investments need to be able to trust that the claimed benefits of equipment and measures are real.

Standardized measurements and verification are a solution. To bridge trust gaps, DNV’s Vessel Technical Index (VTI), introduced under Recommended Practice DNV-RP-0675, provides a normalized, dimensionless propulsion power index that isolates a ship’s technical performance from external factors like weather and speed.

Using the VTI can verify the impact of routine operational measures. The Maritime Forecast reports that for one chartered vessel, sensor data collected before and after hull and propeller cleaning showed a statistically significant VTI reduction from a mean of 1.32 down to 1.14 relative to an “as-new” baseline of 1.00.

This improvement saved approximately 120 tonnes of fuel over a 33-day voyage. At a fuel price of USD 470/tonne, this equated to USD 56,000 in fuel cost savings, four times more than the USD 14,000 cleaning cost.

Alternative fuel technology uptake is surging

In examining ship-fuel trends through the lens of market data, the Maritime Forecast finds a major shift underway in the global order book, with alternative-fuel-capable gross tonnage surging from just 0.4% in 2020 to 5.2% in 2026.

Uptake is highly segmented, driven by different commercial realities and trade routes. Car carriers see the highest share, with 26% being alternative-fuel-capable, followed by cruise ships (19%) and containerships (11%). Bulk carriers (1.1%) and tankers (1.2% to 5%) lag in part due to tramp trading patterns and uncertain bunkering availability.

DNV data shows LNG and methanol dominating alternative fuel systems, though their installed capacity is underutilized.

“Many dual-fuel ships continue to use conventional fuel oils because alternative fuels remain more expensive and regulatory incentives are limited. Their dual-fuel capability therefore provides future flexibility rather than guaranteeing daily use of alternative fuels,” Sekkesæter explains.

Estimating potential demand for low-GHG fuels

To project how these trends are shaping the maritime fuel transition, the Maritime Forecast estimates total potential demand for low-GHG fuels in shipping using two selected regulatory scenarios that bracket the range of possible outcomes for NZF, as shown in the figure below.

By 2050, maritime demand for low-GHG fuels could range from 33 Mtoe to 185 Mtoe depending on regulatory ambition and energy-efficiency uptake. However, total demand across all sectors could exceed 2,200 Mtoe under a net-zero pathway. Aviation, manufacturing, power generation, and road transport are all expected to compete for many of the same fuel molecules and feedstocks.

This competition is particularly intense for biofuels, which are currently among the most economically attractive decarbonization options. Because sustainable biomass availability is inherently limited, growing demand across sectors is likely to increase competition and put upward pressure on fuel costs. DNV’s analysis suggests that higher-cost pathways such as blue fuels and e-fuels will increasingly be needed to balance future demand.

A bottleneck for alternative fuel bunkering

For financiers and insurers evaluating vessel risk, and charterers planning voyages, fuel availability in ports remains a critical factor in determining fuel viability. Encouragingly, the global bunkering vessel fleet is expanding rapidly. Operational LNG bunkering vessels have risen from 25 in 2020 to 67 today, while 24 methanol bunkering vessels are operating and eight are on order. The first dedicated ammonia bunkering vessel recently entered the order book to operate in Singapore.

However, low-GHG fuel bunkering is highly concentrated along major European and East Asian trade routes. The Maritime Forecast also finds that while low-GHG bunkering has occurred at nearly 90 ports globally, the type of fuel available varies dramatically.

Biodiesels, including FAME and HVO, are the most mature and widely distributed, supplied at nearly 70 ports. Liquefied bio-methane is available at 20 ports, mainly in Europe. Low-GHG methanol has been bunkered at 16 ports, concentrated in East Asia and Western Europe. Low-GHG ammonia remains in its infancy, with bunkering reported at only three ports, all in East Asia.

text:
Every last Thursday of September, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) celebrates World Maritime Day, a date dedicated to highlighting the importance of maritime transport, as well as the challenges it faces and the impacts derived from its operations.

This September 24th, this celebration is commemorated under the theme "From Policy to Practice: Driving Maritime Excellence," which, for the first time, will be maintained for two consecutive years (2026 and 2027).

To better understand the current scenario, according to sector reports, global maritime transport moves more than 80% of global merchandise trade, which positions it as a fundamental component for international supply chains. However, this sector is entering a period of fragile growth, increasing costs, and growing uncertainty, noted the United Nations (UN).

In this new edition of World Maritime Day, the IMO highlighted the need for sector standards to move to implementation. To advance in this task, the organization contemplates technical assistance, training, and cooperation among its member states.

From Standards to Decarbonization

Part of the current regulations make it clear that decarbonization continues to be a pending task. Among the main international instruments are the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) and the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL). The latter, through its Annex VI, establishes measures to reduce atmospheric pollution and improve the energy efficiency of vessels.

The need to advance in this direction is reflected in the figures from the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD): during 2024, greenhouse gas emissions from maritime transport increased by 5%; while as of May 2025, only 8% of the global fleet's tonnage was equipped to use alternative fuels.

In addition to existing regulations, there is the proposed IMO Net Zero Framework. The proposal outlines a global standard for the intensity of maritime fuel emissions, as well as an economic mechanism to price greenhouse gas emissions from ships. However, its formal adoption was postponed for a year during last October's negotiations, so it does not yet constitute an international regulation in force.

Major Challenges for the Sector

On the other hand, the IMO also highlighted the effects of international conflicts on navigation and supply chains. Attacks against merchant ships in various conflict zones, including the Strait of Hormuz, have increased risks for crews and disrupted the movement of goods.

"The lives of seafarers are threatened, and the global supply of fuel, fertilizers, and food has been disrupted. These disruptions to the global economy have devastating consequences, especially for developing countries," said António Guterres, United Nations Secretary-General.

Thus, World Maritime Day 2026 makes it clear that the challenges of maritime transport go beyond establishing new commitments. For an industry that sustains a significant part of international trade, the application of existing standards and the development of low-emission technologies will be central elements of its transformation in the coming years.

text:
The number of B100 samples ENGINE recorded in Rotterdam more than doubled in the first eight months of 2026 from a year earlier, lifting its share of the port's biofuel samples to almost a quarter.

ENGINE recorded 77 B100 fuel quality samples in Rotterdam between January and August, up 126% from 34 in the same period last year.

In total, ENGINE had data for 342 biofuel samples in Rotterdam between January and August 2026, up from 275 in the same period of 2025.

ENGINE's sample data covers only part of Rotterdam's biofuel bunker market. In the first half of 2026, suppliers in the Dutch port sold around 345,000 mt of what the Port of Rotterdam Authority classes as bio-blended fuel oils and distillates.

ENGINE's samples for the same period cover around 135,000 mt, or 39%, of those sales. Some samples do not have a quantity recorded, so actual coverage is somewhat higher.

The port authority does not report B100 sales as a separate category, so no official B100 figures exist for the port. The number of B100 samples in ENGINE's data can therefore act as an indicator of how demand for the fuel is trending in Rotterdam.

B100's share of Rotterdam's biofuel samples rose to 23% in the first eight months of 2026, from 12% in the same period of 2025.

Most other biofuel grades lost share. B30-VLSFO accounted for 28% of samples, down from 37%. B30-LSMGO's share slipped from 22% to 20%, and B30-HSFO's fell from 7% to 3%.

B30-ULSFO was the only other grade to gain share, rising from 22% to 27%.

Rotterdam is currently the largest bunker hub in the world by marine biofuel volumes. The port's demand is supported by the Netherlands' implementation of the EU's RED III directive, which incentivises bunkering of biofuels, making them considerably cheaper in Rotterdam than in other European ports.

Under Dutch rules, bunker suppliers in the country's ports can generate maritime emission reduction units, known as ZRE A tickets, by selling low-emission marine fuels such as biofuels made from advanced feedstocks listed in the directive, including palm oil mill effluent.

These ZRE A tickets can then be sold to suppliers of conventional fuels such as VLSFO or LSMGO, who need them to meet their own obligations.

The EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) and FuelEU Maritime add a further pull, as both reward shipowners for burning biofuel with lower carbon costs and smaller compliance penalties.

ENGINE's samples show 15 bunker suppliers selling biofuels in Rotterdam in the first eight months of 2026, up from 10 in the same period last year. The number selling B100 rose from three to seven.

Dutch bunker supplier Verde Marine Energy made its first B100 delivery in the ARA region in June.

text:
International shipping's path toward decarbonization remains under negotiation. Support for an International Maritime Organization-led solution appears to be holding. However, important questions about the pace and design of the transition remain unresolved.

The IMO's Intersessional Working Group on Reduction of Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Ships met September 1–4 to advance discussions surrounding the Net-Zero Framework. Further talks are scheduled for November, followed by the Marine Environment Protection Committee meeting from November 30 to December 3 and an expected Extraordinary Session on December 4.

One possible outcome is a framework that initially imposes less stringent greenhouse gas reduction requirements but later accelerates them. Such a compromise could provide the industry with more time to prepare. But it could also prolong investment uncertainty and increase the importance of bio-bunker fuels as an immediately available decarbonization option.

Key Takeaways

The IMO may adopt less demanding emissions requirements initially, followed by a steeper reduction trajectory toward 2040.

Continued policy uncertainty could delay investment in emerging marine fuels and propulsion technologies.

Available bio-bunker fuels could play a larger transitional role, although uptake will depend on cost, supply, sustainability requirements and competing demand.

Why Could the IMO's Initial Requirements Be Weakened?

The Net-Zero Framework is intended to translate the ambitions of the 2023 IMO GHG Strategy into enforceable requirements. Yet countries continue to disagree over how quickly those requirements should take effect and how the framework's economic elements should operate.

One central issue is the proposed greenhouse gas fuel intensity, or GFI, trajectory. The GFI mechanism would progressively reduce the allowable emissions intensity of energy used aboard ships. This would encourage operators to transition toward lower-carbon fuels and technologies.

According to a Prima CarbonZero market report, several delegations have proposed easing the framework's initial strictness during the early years of implementation. The result could be a more gradual reduction around 2030, followed by a steeper trajectory toward 2040.

This approach may make the framework more manageable at the outset. The concession could serve a particularly important purpose while the availability, scalability and affordability of alternative marine fuels remain uncertain.

But reducing near-term ambition would not necessarily remove the industry's longer-term decarbonization obligation. Instead, it could shift more of the required change into a shorter period.

How Does Regulatory Uncertainty Affect Marine Fuel Investment?

As a recent analyst commentary in Prima CarbonZero notes, shipowners, fuel producers, and infrastructure developers must make investment decisions long before the final shape of future fuel demand is known. Accordingly, uncertainty surrounding the IMO framework affects more than regulatory compliance. It influences which vessels, production facilities, and supply chains receive capital.

The one-year adjournment of the Net-Zero Framework vote in October 2025 reportedly contributed to a slowdown in some investments in low-carbon fuels and propulsion technologies. Continuing disagreements could reinforce that caution, particularly for projects dependent on a clear long-term compliance signal.

A less ambitious initial GFI trajectory could have a similar effect. If near-term compliance pressure is reduced, some market participants may have less incentive to commit immediately to fuels and technologies that require new production capacity, vessel modifications, or specialized infrastructure.

However, delaying those investments could leave the sector facing a more difficult transition as requirements tighten more rapidly.

Could Bio-Bunker Fuels Gain a Larger Transitional Role?

In this environment, available bio-bunker fuels may become increasingly important.

Compared with several emerging marine fuel pathways, certain biofuel blends can be introduced with fewer changes to existing vessels and bunkering infrastructure. This can make them a more accessible option for operators seeking to reduce emissions while preserving flexibility around longer-term fleet and fuel decisions.

A softer initial compliance trajectory would not automatically translate into stronger bio-bunker demand. Actual uptake will also depend on feedstock availability, fuel pricing, sustainability requirements, lifecycle emissions, and competition from road transport, aviation and other sectors.

Nevertheless, prolonged uncertainty around the Net-Zero Framework could extend the period in which drop-in and blended biofuels serve as practical transitional tools. Rather than committing immediately to a single long-term propulsion pathway, some operators may use bio-bunker fuels to achieve incremental emissions reductions. But they must still monitor how regulation, technology, and fuel supply develop.

Which Elements of the Framework Retain Support?

Although important details remain contested, the underlying GFI concept appears to retain broad support. The transfer and pooling of Surplus Units, the mechanisms that would give operators greater flexibility in meeting requirements, also appear less controversial.

The larger disagreements concern how the GFI system should be structured and how demanding its trajectory should be. Discussions include whether the IMO should retain the proposed two-tier approach or adopt a single-tier model similar to FuelEU Maritime.

Behind that technical debate is a more fundamental policy question:

Should regulation be set aggressively enough to stimulate investment and create demand for new fuels, or should its ambition reflect the fuels currently available at scalable and affordable levels?

What Should Marine Fuel Market Participants Watch Next?

The meetings scheduled for November and December will be critical in determining whether countries can reach sufficient agreement on the Net-Zero Framework's final design.

For biofuel producers, traders, bunker suppliers and shipowners, the outcome will help shape both the pace of marine decarbonization and the competitive position of different fuels. A softer beginning could extend the opportunity for available bio-bunker solutions. But it may also set the stage for a sharper compliance challenge later.

The direction of travel remains decarbonization. The unresolved question is how quickly the industry will be required to move and which fuels will be best positioned to bridge the gap.

Track the Marine Biofuels Market Month by Month

As the IMO negotiations continue, marine fuel market participants will need to follow more than the final policy outcome. Shifts in regulation, regional demand, biofuel and feedstock pricing, and supply availability will all influence the role bio-bunker fuels can realistically play.

title: Trump Renews Opposition to IMO Net-Zero Shipping Framework at UN - MARINO PH
description:
US President Donald Trump has renewed his opposition to the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework, criticizing the proposed global greenhouse gas emissions pricing mechanism during his address to the United Nations General Assembly on September 22.
Trump described the measure as a potential “global carbon tax,” claiming it could increase international shipping costs by 10% to 20% or more.
His administration has maintained that there should be no global taxation imposed through the IMO.
The IMO framework would introduce progressively stricter greenhouse gas fuel-intensity requirements for ships, alongside an economic mechanism requiring higher-emitting vessels to make compliance payments while providing incentives for lower-emission ships.
Further negotiations are scheduled before the framework returns for possible adoption at an extraordinary MEPC session on December 4, 2026.

US President Donald Trump has renewed his opposition to the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework, criticizing the proposed global greenhouse gas emissions pricing mechanism during his address to the United Nations General Assembly on September 22.

Trump described the measure as a potential “global carbon tax,” claiming it could increase international shipping costs by 10% to 20% or more. His administration has maintained that there should be no global taxation imposed through the IMO.

The IMO framework would introduce progressively stricter greenhouse gas fuel-intensity requirements for ships, alongside an economic mechanism requiring higher-emitting vessels to make compliance payments while providing incentives for lower-emission ships.

The framework was initially approved in April 2025, but its adoption was postponed for one year after member states failed to reach agreement. Further negotiations are scheduled before the framework returns for possible adoption at an extraordinary MEPC session on December 4, 2026.
